meta.title: Who really said "Everybody Talks About the Weather, But Nobody Does Anything About It"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Mark Twain never wrote it. Quote Investigator traces the weather quip to his Hartford friend Charles Dudley Warner, credited in print from 1884.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Everybody Talks About the Weather, But Nobody Does Anything About It'?
meta.ogDescription: Twain gets the credit; the evidence points to Charles Dudley Warner, whose weather quip was in print by 1884. Twain's name appears only from 1905.

answer.label: Not Mark Twain — most likely Charles Dudley Warner
answer.authorDates: 1829–1900 · American essayist, novelist & co-editor of the Hartford Courant
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator concludes that “the preponderance of the evidence indicates that Charles Dudley Warner crafted the weather maxim,” with versions credited to him in print from 1884 onward and the Twain credit appearing only from 1905. Twain’s own name is attached to no primary text: Respectfully Quoted records that the saying “has never been verified in his writings.”
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — the wording was never fixed, and no single printing can be called the original.

source.excerpt: A well known American writer said once that, while everybody talked about the weather, nobody seemed to do anything about it.
trail: 1884 — the earliest version located by Quote Investigator ↗, in the New York Chamber of Commerce proceedings: a speaker recalls “the observation of my old friend and partner, DUDLEY WARNER, concerning New-England weather — it is a matter about which a great deal is said, but very little done.”

August 1897 — an unsigned Hartford Courant editorial prints the familiar shape but credits an unnamed “well known American writer.” Respectfully Quoted ↗ holds that Warner wrote it. (The date is recorded as 24 August by Quote Investigator’s citation and as 27 August by Respectfully Quoted.)

1904 — William Dean Howells’s Harper’s “Editor’s Easy Chair” tribute, reprinted at page 206 of Annie Fields’s memoir of Warner ↗, puts the joke in Warner’s mouth: “Everybody is talking about the weather, why doesn’t somebody do something?”

1905 onward — the first credits to Mark Twain appear, and by 1910 the New York Times is attributing it to “the late Mark Twain.” In 1912 the Courant answers back: “Mr. Warner once remarked that everybody talks about the weather but nobody seems to do anything about it” (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.excerptNote: The 1897 Hartford Courant editorial — the citation that launched a century of confusion. It was unsigned, Warner was writing the paper’s editorials at the time, and it credits the line to a writer it declines to name. Fifteen years later the same paper named him.

source.rightsNote: Every documented printing of this saying — the 1884 Chamber of Commerce proceedings, the 1889 Book Buyer, the 1897 and 1912 Hartford Courant, Howells’s tribute as reprinted in Annie Fields’s 1904 memoir — is an American work published long before 1931, so all of it is in the public domain in the United States. Warner himself died in 1900. The polished modern wording is a proverbial refinement with no identifiable later claimant.

author.name: Charles Dudley Warner
author.kicker: The friend who lost his best line
author.heading: Who was Charles Dudley Warner?
author.metaLine: 1829–1900 · American essayist, novelist & Hartford Courant editor
author.bio: Charles Dudley Warner co-edited the Hartford Courant from 1867 and became one of the best-known American essayists of his generation, on the strength of gently comic books such as My Summer in a Garden and Being a Boy. He was Mark Twain’s Hartford neighbour, close friend and collaborator — the two wrote The Gilded Age: A Tale of To-day (1873) together, and gave an era its name. His wit survives mostly as remembered talk rather than printed text, which is precisely how his most famous line came loose from him.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and who earned it
misattribution.intro: This may be the single most reliably mis-credited sentence in American humour. It is printed under Twain’s name on mugs, in newscasts and in quotation dictionaries — and it is not in his work.

items.why: The Library of Congress reference Respectfully Quoted states flatly: “Generally, but perhaps mistakenly, attributed to MARK TWAIN. It has never been verified in his writings. Many quotation dictionaries credit Charles Dudley Warner, a friend of Twain’s, with this remark.” (entry 1982 ↗). A full-text search of Mark Twain’s Speeches ↗, which includes his New England weather address, turns up no version of it either.

The unsigned Hartford Courant editorial of August 1897 says only that “a well known American writer said once that, while everybody talked about the weather, nobody seemed to do anything about it.” The Yale Book of Quotations, as quoted by Quote Investigator ↗, notes the writer “is usually taken to be Twain, but the writer could also have been Charles Dudley Warner” — who was writing the paper’s editorials at the time.

Warner’s recorded versions are looser: “a matter about which a great deal is said, but very little done” (1884), and “Everybody is talking about the weather, why doesn’t somebody do something?” in the tribute reprinted in Annie Fields’s 1904 memoir ↗. The neat modern balance belongs to a century of repetition, not to a single page.

Robert U. Johnson’s Remembered Yesterdays (1923) is quoted in Respectfully Quoted ↗ as saying: “Nor have I ever seen in print Mark’s saying about the weather.” Even Twain’s friends could only remember him repeating it.

misattribution.truthLine: The saying is Warner’s: versions are credited to him in print from 1884, and his own newspaper settled it in 1912 — “Mr. Warner once remarked that everybody talks about the weather but nobody seems to do anything about it” (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why it stuck to Twain
lead: Warner and Twain shared a Hartford neighbourhood, a publisher, a circle of friends and, in 1873, a book — The Gilded Age. When a witty nineteenth-century American remark goes looking for an owner, Twain is the gravity well it falls into, and this one had less distance to travel than most: it was already circulating inside Twain’s own social world.

Twain also had a prior claim on the subject. His after-dinner address on New England weather — printed as “The Weather” in Mark Twain’s Speeches ↗ — is a sustained comic riff on exactly this theme. It does not contain the famous sentence anywhere. But once the public filed “funny man, New England weather” under Twain, the sentence found its way into the same folder.
detailsBody: The line survives in at least four shapes. In 1884 it is “a matter about which a great deal is said, but very little done.” In 1897 it is “while everybody talked about the weather, nobody seemed to do anything about it.” In Howells’s memorial tribute it is “Everybody is talking about the weather, why doesn’t somebody do something?” The 1912 Hartford Courant gives it in nearly the modern form: “Mr. Warner once remarked that everybody talks about the weather but nobody seems to do anything about it.”

That drift is itself the evidence. A line reported this many ways, by this many people, is a line that was spoken and remembered rather than composed on a page — which is why no manuscript will ever settle it, and why the tidy version everyone quotes today belongs to no one printing in particular.
context.pull: A remark that was never written down properly, made by a man who lived next door to a legend.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes 'the preponderance of the evidence indicates that Charles Dudley Warner crafted the weather maxim'; documents an 1884 New York Chamber of Commerce citation ('a matter about which a great deal is said, but very little done'), an 1889 Book Buyer citation, the August 1897 Hartford Courant editorial ('A well known American writer said once that, while everybody talked about the weather, nobody seemed to do anything about it'), the 1901/1904 Warner profile ('Everybody is talking about the weather; why doesn't somebody do something?'), a 1903 Century Magazine piece by Joseph H. Twichell, a first Twain credit in 1905, a 1910 New York Times Twain credit, and the 1912 Hartford Courant line 'Mr. Warner once remarked that everybody talks about the weather but nobody seems to do anything about it.' Its footnote dates the Courant editorial 24 August 1897, p. 8. It also quotes the Yale Book of Quotations that the 'well-known American writer' is usually taken to be Twain but could have been Warner.

Respectfully Quoted (entry 1982) states: 'Generally, but perhaps mistakenly, attributed to MARK TWAIN. It has never been verified in his writings. Many quotation dictionaries credit Charles Dudley Warner, a friend of Twain's, with this remark. But what Warner actually wrote, in an editorial in the Hartford (Connecticut) Courant, August 27, 1897, p. 8, was: "A well known American writer said once that, while everybody talked about the weather, nobody seemed to do anything about it."' It also quotes Robert U. Johnson, Remembered Yesterdays, p. 322 (1923): 'Nor have I ever seen in print Mark's saying about the weather...'

Annie Fields, Charles Dudley Warner (1904), p. 206 reprints Howells's 'Editor's Easy Chair' tribute from Harper's Magazine, which records: 'When people were once tried almost beyond endurance by the most exasperating of winters, he said, "Everybody is talking about the weather, why doesn't somebody do something?"' — 'he' being Warner. The book explicitly identifies the tribute as Howells's Easy Chair piece published after Warner's death.

Mark Twain's Speeches (1910) contains 'The Weather', his address to the New England Society's annual dinner, which riffs at length on New England weather; a full-text search of the volume returns no instance of 'nobody does anything about it', 'talks about the weather' or any equivalent version of the famous line.

Wikiquote's Charles Dudley Warner page carries the quote 'A well known American writer said once that, while everybody talked about the weather, nobody seemed to do anything about it,' cited to an editorial in the Hartford Courant (27 August 1897), notes the variant 'Everybody complains about the weather, but nobody does anything about it,' and notes it has become often attributed to Mark Twain.

Wikipedia gives Charles Dudley Warner's dates as 12 September 1829 – 20 October 1900, describes him as an American essayist, novelist and editor, co-editor of the Hartford Courant from 1867, co-author with Mark Twain of The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today (1873), and credits him with the weather quip while noting it is still commonly misattributed to Twain.

This Day in Quotes states the Hartford Courant editorial was published 24 August 1897, that it was unsigned, that Warner was writing the paper's editorials at the time and probably wrote it, and that the editorial credits the saying to someone else in wording slightly different from the familiar version.
